paper: Gander & Stuart 1998 — Space-Time Continuous Analysis of Waveform Relaxation for the Heat Equation (SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 19(6):2014–2031, DOI 10.1137/S1064827596305337)

open_questions.q: How tight is the Theorem 3.10 upper bound 1 − 4r(1−r)sin²(π/(2(N+1))) across the (N, r) plane, and does the measured-to-bound ratio stay bounded away from 1 as N grows or as the overlap fraction r → 0?
open_questions.basis: Our C3 replication tested only a single configuration (N=8, r=0.35): predicted upper bound 0.9726, measured decay 0.9327, so measured/bound ≈ 0.96. The paper states Theorem 3.10 gives an upper bound (not an equality), and we do not know whether the gap between measured contraction and this bound is a fixed multiplicative factor, scales with N, or collapses in the small-overlap limit r → 0 where the bound approaches 1 by construction.
open_questions.next_steps: Rerun run_N_subdomain over a grid, e.g. N ∈ {2,4,8,16,32} × r ∈ {0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.35, 0.50}, snap overlaps to Δx=Δt=0.01, and report a heat-map of measured/bound. Then check whether the pattern is consistent with a heuristic sharp rate (e.g. does measured = 1 − c(N)·r(1−r)sin²(π/(2(N+1))) for some slowly varying c(N)?), and flag any (N, r) regime where the bound becomes essentially vacuous.

open_questions.q: Does the space-time continuous rate ρ = α(1−β)/(β(1−α)) survive a bounded time window T under a Gauss–Seidel-style (sequential) SWR sweep, and how does the finite-T superlinear regime match the Jacobi-style parallel sweep we tested?
open_questions.basis: The paper's Theorem 2.4/2.8 gives linear contraction on the infinite time interval; on bounded intervals classical WR theory admits a faster superlinear phase. We only implemented and measured the Jacobi-parallel update (run_two_subdomain, run_N_subdomain), and only compared against the infinite-time linear rate. We do not know from our runs whether a Gauss–Seidel sweep exhibits a distinct pre-asymptotic superlinear regime on the paper's T=3 test problem, or whether it just changes the pre-factor.
open_questions.next_steps: Add a Gauss–Seidel variant of solve_subdomain that consumes the just-updated neighbor trace within the same iteration, rerun the (0.4,0.6) two-subdomain problem for T ∈ {0.5, 1, 3, 10, 100}, and fit both the asymptotic (large-k) rate and any early superlinear phase. Compare against Jacobi at matched cost per iteration; verify the asymptotic factor still equals ρ.

open_questions.q: Is the mesh-robustness of the contraction factor (C2) truly a property of the physical-space overlap alone, or is it partly conditional on the backward-Euler + centered-FD combination we (and the paper) used?
open_questions.basis: We measured 0.4439 to four significant figures across Δx=Δt from 0.02 down to 0.0025 with backward Euler / centered FD, exactly matching the paper's discretization. The paper's theory is space-time continuous, so the result should be discretization-agnostic in the limit, but we have not verified that Crank–Nicolson, BDF2, higher-order spatial FD, or a spectral spatial discretization all give the same 0.4439 under refinement. If they do not, the mesh-robustness observation is partly an artifact of matching the paper's discretization.
open_questions.next_steps: Reimplement solve_full and solve_subdomain with (a) Crank–Nicolson, (b) BDF2, (c) fourth-order compact FD in space. Rerun the mesh_robust sweep at fixed overlap (0.4,0.6). Report the measured contraction factor as a function of Δx for each discretization; expect all to converge to ρ=0.4444, and quantify the pre-asymptotic gap.

open_questions.q: How does the initial guess shape both the stagnation length and the achievable per-iteration rate in the multi-subdomain case?
open_questions.basis: We reproduced the ~4-iteration stagnation phase in the 8-subdomain, 35%-overlap run using the paper's constant-in-time initial guess (equal to the IC value). The paper remarks qualitatively that 'the error stagnates since information has to be propagated across domains,' but neither the paper nor our runs characterise how the stagnation length changes under different starts (e.g. a coarse-grid warm start, a random start bounded by ‖IC‖, or a nonzero-source-aware initial trace).
open_questions.next_steps: Rerun run_N_subdomain (N=8, r=0.35) with initial guesses (i) constant = IC (baseline), (ii) linear-in-t interpolation between the two Dirichlet BCs at every interface, (iii) trace from a coarse-mesh full-domain solve on 4× coarser grid, (iv) small-amplitude random perturbation of the baseline. Report stagnation length (first iteration k such that error ratio < 0.99) and the asymptotic per-double-iteration factor for each; check whether the asymptotic factor is invariant (as theory predicts) while stagnation length varies.

open_questions.q: Does the space-time continuous overlap-in-space contraction rate framework extend cleanly to 2D or 3D heat equations with non-strip subdomain geometries (e.g. cross-points, non-convex overlaps), and if so does an analogous ρ formula involving geometric ratios of the overlap survive?
open_questions.basis: Both the paper's analysis and our reproduction are strictly 1D (Ω = [0,L]) with strip subdomains and a clean overlap interval [α, β]. The paper's contribution is fundamentally the space-time continuous perspective for overlapping Schwarz WR; whether the same style of proof yields a rate that is (a) still robust to mesh refinement and (b) still a simple algebraic function of overlap geometry in 2D with corner-adjacent subdomains (T-junctions, cross-points) is not addressed in this paper and not tested in our replication.
open_questions.next_steps: Implement a 2D backward-Euler heat solver on the unit square with a 2×2 overlapping subdomain decomposition (each subdomain a rectangle with a small overlap band on each internal edge, generating one cross-point). Measure the per-double-iteration contraction of the maximum interface error under fixed physical overlap while refining a uniform Cartesian mesh from h=1/32 down to h=1/256. Compare (i) whether the rate is mesh-robust, (ii) whether it is well-approximated by the 1D formula applied edge-by-edge, and (iii) whether the cross-point induces additional stagnation. This clarifies whether Gander–Stuart 1998 is genuinely a 1D result or the intrinsic 1D projection of a broader multi-dimensional theorem.
